news.2026-10-11-azerbaidjan-banque-mondi: Azerbaijan: the World Bank cuts its growth forecast to 1.2%
The Caucasus country, which lives off oil and gas, will grow less than expected in 2026. Declining oil fields weigh on the economy, and the state is spending less on building projects.
In its October update, the World Bank forecasts growth of 1.2% in 2026 for Azerbaijan, then 1.8% in 2027 and 1.9% in 2028 [1].
It blames the slowdown on the structural decline of the oil sector and on non-oil activity that is weaker than expected, after cuts in state investment spending [1].
This is a cut from April, when the bank was expecting 2% for 2026 [2]. Azerbaijan's central bank, for its part, was forecasting 1.1% in May [1].
A country that depends on oil sees its income melt away when its wells produce less. Azerbaijan is therefore trying to grow other sectors (trade, construction, services), but that takes time.
The country is also a piece of Europe's energy puzzle: it sends gas to Europe by pipeline. Its economy therefore matters beyond the Caucasus.
This doesn't change your daily life right away. But it is a reminder: the gas that heats part of Europe comes from countries whose economies are fragile and very dependent on this single resource.

news.2026-10-11-angola-banque-mondiale.t: Angola: expensive oil lifts forecast growth to 4.5%
news.2026-10-11-angola-banque-mondiale.s: The World Bank sharply raises its forecast for Angola. The country exports oil, so it benefits from higher prices instead of suffering from them.
news.2026-10-11-angola-banque-mondiale.p: The World Bank has raised its 2026 growth forecast for Angola to 4.5%, versus 3.1% in 2025. It then expects 3.3% in 2027 and 3.1% in 2028 [1].
It credits the rise to oil exports and high crude prices [1].

The country is less exposed than others to the energy shock linked to the conflict in the Middle East, because it sells oil instead of buying it [1]. The bank expects inflation to fall to 10.3% this year [1].
news.2026-10-11-angola-banque-mondiale.w: When oil rises, countries that buy it pay more, and those that sell it earn more. Angola is in the second group: its budget depends largely on crude.
Even with 4.5%, inflation above 10% remains heavy for residents: prices rise fast, so purchasing power does not always keep up with growth.
news.2026-10-11-angola-banque-mondiale.f: Filling up your car costs more, but for some producing countries it is good news. The same event creates winners and losers depending on whether a country sells or buys oil.

news.2026-10-11-mongolie-bad.geo.0.label: Mongolia
news.2026-10-11-mongolie-bad.title: Mongolia: the Asian Development Bank plans $1.3 billion by 2027
news.2026-10-11-mongolie-bad.summary: The bank's president came to Ulaanbaatar. Three loans worth $455 million in total were signed for health, schools and natural disasters.
news.2026-10-11-mongolie-bad.points.0: The president of the Asian Development Bank (ADB), Masato Kanda, announced a planned package of $1.3 billion for Mongolia by 2027, during a visit in early October [1].
news.2026-10-11-mongolie-bad.points.1: Three loan agreements were signed, for $455 million in all: $225 million for provincial health services, $130 million for education during economic hardship, and $100 million to better cope with disasters [1].
news.2026-10-11-mongolie-bad.points.2: He also met Mongolia's president and its finance minister, and visited a herder family about 54 kilometers from the capital [1].
news.2026-10-11-mongolie-bad.why.0: Mongolia is a large, sparsely populated country squeezed between Russia and China. It relies on outside financial partners to modernize its public services.
news.2026-10-11-mongolie-bad.why.1: The $1.3 billion is a plan through 2027, not a transfer already made: only the $455 million is signed for now.
news.2026-10-11-mongolie-bad.forMe: No direct effect on your wallet. But it is an example of how development banks finance schools, hospitals and disaster prevention in countries the media rarely mention.
news.2026-10-11-mongolie-bad.figures.0.l: the package planned for Mongolia by 2027
news.2026-10-11-mongolie-bad.figures.1.l: the three loans signed during the visit
news.2026-10-11-oman-sp-croissance.title: Oman: the country that exports without going through Hormuz sees growth forecast at 3.5%
news.2026-10-11-oman-sp-croissance.summa: Rating agency S&P sharply raises its forecast for Oman. Its ports face the Arabian Sea, not the blocked strait.
news.2026-10-11-oman-sp-croissance.point: Rating agency S&P Global Ratings raised its 2026 growth forecast for Oman to 3.5%, from 1.6% before, and confirmed the country's BBB- rating with a stable outlook [1][2].

A large part of Oman's export infrastructure for crude, liquefied natural gas and refined products faces the Gulf of Oman or the Arabian Sea directly, which reduces its dependence on passage through Hormuz [1].
S&P expects average production of 1.1 million barrels a day in 2026. It warns that its forecasts would be cut if Iran stepped up its attacks on Omani infrastructure [1][2].
news.2026-10-11-oman-sp-croissance.why.0: The Strait of Hormuz is the bottleneck through which a large share of Gulf oil passes. When it is blocked, countries with no other outlet lose their income.
news.2026-10-11-oman-sp-croissance.why.1: Oman is lucky in its geography. For comparison, a Reuters poll in July saw Kuwait and Qatar, entirely dependent on Hormuz, shrinking by 8.1% this year [3].
news.2026-10-11-oman-sp-croissance.forMe: When a shipping route closes, oil and gas get more expensive everywhere. Countries with another outlet, like Oman, become more valuable suppliers for buyers, including Europe.
news.2026-10-11-oman-sp-croissance.figur: Oman's expected growth in 2026, versus 1.6% before the revision

news.2026-10-11-ouzbekistan-envois-argen: Uzbekistan: migrants sent $9.3 billion in six months
Money sent home by Uzbeks working abroad weighs heavily on the country's economy. It increasingly comes from the United Kingdom and the European Union.
According to the central bank, transfers from abroad to Uzbekistan reached $9.3 billion from January to June 2026, 13% more than a year earlier [1].
Transfers from the United Kingdom jumped 62%, those from the European Union 27% and those from the United States 19% [1].
Card-to-card transfers grew 32% to reach $4.8 billion, a little over half of the total [2].
Many Uzbeks go abroad to work and send money to their families. For the country, it is a very important source of foreign currency that supports millions of households.
The fact that transfers are growing fast from the United Kingdom and the European Union shows that Uzbeks are going to work in a wider range of countries.
If you send or receive money from a relative abroad, you are part of this worldwide movement: such transfers often weigh more than official development aid in many countries.

news.2026-10-11-uruguay-recul-pib.title: Uruguay: the economy shrinks 0.8% in the second quarter, drought to blame
news.2026-10-11-uruguay-recul-pib.summar: The small South American country, often cited for its stability, sees its activity fall. Agriculture suffered from the lack of water.
news.2026-10-11-uruguay-recul-pib.points: Uruguay's central bank says activity fell 0.8% in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the previous quarter, and 0.5% over one year [1].
The sharp fall in agriculture is blamed on the drought that hit summer crops in the last harvest [1].
The Ministry of Economy keeps a growth forecast of 1.6% for 2026, already reduced from 2.2%, while the median of private analysts falls to 1% [1][2].
news.2026-10-11-uruguay-recul-pib.why.0: When a country lives largely off agricultural exports, the weather directly affects its economy: a smaller harvest means fewer sales and less growth.
news.2026-10-11-uruguay-recul-pib.why.1: The gap between the government's forecast and the analysts' shows there is still uncertainty about the rest of the year.
news.2026-10-11-uruguay-recul-pib.forMe: Uruguay exports meat, soybeans and dairy products. A bad harvest there may one day show up in some prices abroad, even if the effect on you is small.
news.2026-10-11-uruguay-recul-pib.figure: Uruguay's activity in Q2 2026, over three months

Honduras: inflation at 6.2%, the central bank raises its rate
Honduras has the highest inflation in Central America. Its central bank has raised its policy rate by 0.25 points.

In August 2026, inflation in Honduras reached 6.20% year on year, the highest in the region, ahead of the Dominican Republic (5.13%) and Guatemala (3.37%) [1]. Costa Rica is the opposite case: its prices fell 0.17% over one year [1].
On September 18, Honduras's central bank raised its policy rate from 5.75% to 6%, effective September 21. Its inflation target is 4% [2].
It cites higher oil and food prices worldwide, made worse by conflicts and tariffs. It presents the move as preventive [2].
A higher policy rate makes credit more expensive: loans to households and businesses cost more, which slows price rises but also activity.
The contrast with Costa Rica, a neighbor where prices are falling, shows that inflation is not the same everywhere, even in a small region.
Expensive oil doesn't only hit Europe: it pushes prices up in countries with much lower incomes, where fuel and food weigh more in the budget.

news.2026-10-11-pologne-croatie-inflatio: Poland and Croatia: inflation picks up in September, driven by fuel
In Poland, prices are rising 4.0% over a year. In Croatia, the flash estimate gives 4.7%. In both cases, energy is the cause.
In Poland, inflation rose to 4.0% year on year in September. Fuel for private transport rose 36.1%, and electricity, gas and other fuels 4.9% [1].
In Croatia, the flash estimate of September inflation is 4.7% year on year [1]. It was 4.2% in August, and the rise comes mainly from energy, up 20.5% [2].
The recent Croatian high goes back to May, at 5.2% [2]. Caution: a flash estimate can be revised when the final figure is released.
Inflation is the general rise in prices. When fuel becomes much more expensive, everything that has to be transported rises too, and the increase gradually spreads to the rest.
Croatia, a eurozone member, and Poland, which keeps its own currency, have different central banks. But they are hit by the same shock from energy.
If you go on vacation in Croatia or Poland, local prices are higher than a year ago. The figure also reminds us that expensive fuel hits all of Europe, not only France.

news.2026-10-12-ouzbekistan-inflation.ti: Uzbekistan: inflation slows to 6.4%, central bank keeps its rate at 14%
news.2026-10-12-ouzbekistan-inflation.su: Prices are rising more slowly than a year ago in Uzbekistan. The central bank stays cautious and is not cutting rates yet.
news.2026-10-12-ouzbekistan-inflation.po: In September, Uzbek inflation is 6.4% over one year, versus 8% a year earlier [1].
Excluding fruit and vegetables, it reaches 6.8% over one year [1].
On September 16, the central bank kept its key rate at 14%; it wants to bring inflation down to 5% by the end of 2027, and its next meeting is on October 28 [2].
news.2026-10-12-ouzbekistan-inflation.wh: Inflation is the general rise in prices. A high key rate, like the 14% here, makes credit expensive and slows prices down. As long as inflation stays above the 5% target, the central bank does not want to ease up.
Uzbekistan is a Central Asian country. As long as prices rise faster than the target, the central bank keeps rates high, which makes loans expensive for companies.
news.2026-10-12-ouzbekistan-inflation.fo: You are not directly affected. But it is an example of a country fighting rising prices with very high interest rates, a recipe many emerging economies use.

news.2026-10-12-mongolie-taux.title: Mongolia: rate held at 12.5% as inflation tops 12%
news.2026-10-12-mongolie-taux.summary: Prices in Mongolia are rising very fast, driven by fuel and food. The central bank pauses after raising its rate in August.
news.2026-10-12-mongolie-taux.points.0: Mongolia's central bank kept its key rate at 12.5% at its September meeting, after raising it by 0.5 points in August [1].
news.2026-10-12-mongolie-taux.points.1: Inflation stood at 12.5% in August, after a peak of 13% in July; core inflation (excluding the most volatile prices) is 6.8% [1].
news.2026-10-12-mongolie-taux.points.2: The central bank expects a gradual decline from the second quarter of 2027 and cites as risks fuel and food prices linked to the Middle East conflict, as well as public finances [1].
news.2026-10-12-mongolie-taux.why.0: When there is a big gap between headline inflation (12.5%) and core inflation (6.8%), it means a few very expensive items are pulling everything up, here fuel and food.
news.2026-10-12-mongolie-taux.why.1: Mongolia imports most of its fuel: an expensive barrel quickly feeds into everyday prices. It is a landlocked country, squeezed between China and Russia.
news.2026-10-12-mongolie-taux.forMe: You will not see it in your daily life. But it shows that the oil surge coming from the Gulf reaches the heart of Asia, far from any port.

news.2026-10-12-ouganda-shilling.title: Uganda: the shilling hits a record low, above 4,000 to the dollar
news.2026-10-12-ouganda-shilling.summary: The Ugandan currency has never been worth so little. Fuel importers are buying dollars, and the central bank is letting it happen.
In early October, the Ugandan shilling went past 4,000 to the dollar, its lowest level ever recorded; it reached 4,025 at the start of trading on Monday [1][2].
It has lost about 10% since January, the second-worst performance in Africa this year after Ghana's cedi [1].

Currency dealers point to dollar buying by manufacturers, energy importers and traders preparing end-of-year imports, in a context of expensive oil. The central bank did not step in and says the currency's value depends on supply and demand [2].
news.2026-10-12-ouganda-shilling.why.0: A falling currency makes everything imported more expensive. Uganda has to buy its fuel in dollars: the pricier the dollar, the more petrol, transport and food cost in shillings.
news.2026-10-12-ouganda-shilling.why.1: The central bank could sell dollars to slow the fall, but it keeps its reserves and lets the market decide. It is a choice: not spending its reserves, at the risk of seeing prices rise.
news.2026-10-12-ouganda-shilling.forMe: You do not pay in shillings. But Uganda exports coffee and gold, and a weak currency changes the prices it can offer. It also affects Ugandans abroad who send money home.
news.2026-10-12-ouganda-shilling.figures: shillings to the dollar, a record, at the start of trading on Monday

news.2026-10-12-uruguay-inflation.title: Uruguay: inflation rises to 4.68%, slightly above target
news.2026-10-12-uruguay-inflation.summar: Prices in Uruguay rose a little faster in September, driven by food, but stay within the zone tolerated by the central bank.
news.2026-10-12-uruguay-inflation.points: The statistics institute published September inflation on October 5: 4.68% over one year, versus 4.55% in August [1].
The central bank's target is 4.5%, with a tolerance zone of 3% to 6%; the figure is therefore above target but within the zone [1].
Over the month, prices rose 0.54%, mostly because of tomatoes, onions and meat; core inflation is 4.47% [1].
news.2026-10-12-uruguay-inflation.why.0: A central bank aims for a given pace of price rises. Here, food (vegetables, meat) weighed on the index: when these products rise, it shows up immediately in the figure.
news.2026-10-12-uruguay-inflation.why.1: Uruguay is a small South American country. Its central bank uses interest rates, not price controls, to keep inflation close to target.
news.2026-10-12-uruguay-inflation.forMe: If you eat South American beef, the price it reaches here depends partly on what happens in these markets. Uruguay is one of the region's major meat exporters.
news.2026-10-12-uruguay-inflation.figure: inflation in Uruguay in September 2026, over one year

news.2026-10-12-bulgarie-inflation.title: Bulgaria: inflation rises to 5.6%, well above the eurozone
news.2026-10-12-bulgarie-inflation.summa: In a country that has adopted the euro, prices are climbing faster than in the eurozone as a whole.
news.2026-10-12-bulgarie-inflation.point: According to Eurostat's estimate, Bulgarian inflation is 5.6% over one year in September, versus 5.1% in August [1][2].
In the eurozone as a whole, it is 3.8% in September [1].
news.2026-10-12-bulgarie-inflation.why.0: Joining the eurozone means using the same currency and the same central bank as Germany or France. Bulgaria can therefore no longer raise its rates alone to slow prices.
news.2026-10-12-bulgarie-inflation.why.1: When a country's inflation stays well above the zone's, it is a test of residents' trust in the new currency.
news.2026-10-12-bulgarie-inflation.forMe: Bulgaria is a popular holiday destination and a country where French companies have sites. There, the cost of living is rising faster than at home.
news.2026-10-12-bulgarie-inflation.figur: inflation in the eurozone, same month
news.2026-10-12-hongrie-inflation.title: Hungary: inflation rises to 1.6% and the target will drop to 2.5% in 2028
news.2026-10-12-hongrie-inflation.summar: Hungary has one of the lowest inflation rates in the region, but it is picking up again. The government also wants to lower its target.
news.2026-10-12-hongrie-inflation.points: Hungarian inflation is 1.6% over one year in September, versus 1.3% in August [1].
According to FXStreet's analysis, Hungary will lower its inflation target to 2.5% from 2028 [2].
news.2026-10-12-hongrie-inflation.why.0: A lower inflation target is a firmer promise: prices will have to rise more slowly in the future.
news.2026-10-12-hongrie-inflation.why.1: Hungary stays outside the eurozone and keeps its currency, the forint. Energy increases weigh on prices there, even if the figure remains modest.
news.2026-10-12-hongrie-inflation.forMe: If you travel to Budapest, prices there are stable for now. But the rise in energy also affects Hungarian car factories, which work for European brands.
news.2026-10-12-hongrie-inflation.figure: inflation in Hungary in September 2026, over one year
news.2026-10-12-arabie-houthis-aeroports: Saudi Arabia: four days of Houthi strikes on airports ground hundreds of flights
Yemen's Houthi rebels are targeting Saudi airports, including Riyadh's. The risk to Gulf oil moves the markets.
According to Enterprise (citing Reuters), four days of Houthi strikes on Saudi airports killed three people and grounded hundreds of flights [1].

The Houthis say they fired a missile at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, a day after an attack on the same airport that killed one person. The coalition says it intercepted two missiles over the capital; debris hit a kindergarten and a clinic [1].
In late September, oil had already jumped after attacks claimed by the Houthis on Saudi sites [2]. In early October, Brent was above $102 a barrel [3].
The Houthis are an armed group in Yemen, backed by Iran. Hitting a country's airports means hitting its economic life: travellers, freight, image with investors.
Saudi Arabia is one of the world's biggest oil producers. Every attack on its sites raises fears for supply, and prices react even if production is not hit.
When oil rises, petrol and diesel also rise at the pump in France, with a delay of a few weeks. If you plan a trip with a stopover in the Gulf, also check the state of air traffic.

news.2026-10-12-ormuz-navette-petroliere: Hormuz: Iran threatens the secret "shuttle" carrying oil out of the Gulf
To get around the blocked Strait of Hormuz, the Emirates are moving their oil on small tankers that make round trips. Tehran says it is now targeting them.

On Sunday evening, Iranian official Mohsen Rezaei said that the oil "shuttle" organized by the United States and the United Arab Emirates through the Strait of Hormuz was now an explicit target of Iran. He claims that Iran has been striking five or six of these ships every night for weeks, which has not been independently verified [1].

The day before, attacks around the strait had flared up again as mediation to end the war against Iran is stalled; the US military released a video of a fighter jet bombing a Panama-flagged cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its blockade of Iranian ports [2].

How it works: since April, the Emirati oil group ADNOC has been using "shuttle" tankers that carry crude to the Gulf of Oman, where it is transferred onto large tankers; about 2.5 million barrels per day were expected to move this way in September, close to 40% of the volumes still passing through Hormuz [3]. Each round trip would cost $30–40 million, or $15–20 more per barrel before insurance [4].

The Strait of Hormuz is the exit door for Gulf oil: before the war, about a fifth of the world's oil and gas passed through it, and it has been largely closed since the US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28 [1].

The "shuttle" is a workaround invented to keep exporting despite everything. By naming it a target, Iran is aiming at the last pipe that still works. If this system stops, part of the world's oil supply disappears from the market again.
This story also shows that a war can be fought over logistics: small boats, transfers at sea, insurance premiums. Each step adds a cost that the final buyer ends up paying.

The price of gasoline in France depends on the world price of oil. If Iran manages to cut this shuttle, the barrel could rise, and the fill-up with it, a few weeks later. Even if nothing happens, this costly detour is already part of the price you pay.

news.2026-10-12-algerie-maroc-61-arresta: Algeria: 61 Moroccans arrested over "sabotage", the Maghreb's cold war heats up

Algiers says it has dismantled a network of 61 Moroccans who entered the country illegally to carry out sabotage. No target or weapon has been presented, and the border between the two neighbors has been closed since 1994.

Algerian police announced on Sunday the arrest of 61 Moroccans, including a former soldier, suspected of preparing "acts of sabotage"; according to them, they arrived in Tunis by plane, then entered Algeria illegally through the forests and mountains of El Kala before heading to Oran [1].

The police say they seized Moroccan passports and money in dirhams and euros, but the statement specifies neither the intended targets nor the nature of the planned actions, and does not mention weapons [1]. Moroccan media question the evidence [4].

Back in August, Algeria had announced the arrest of four Moroccans accused of wanting to sabotage its July 2 legislative elections; the land border has been closed since 1994 and Algiers cut diplomatic relations with Rabat in 2021 [2]. Several analyses point to a role for the United Arab Emirates, with no published proof, while Algiers also cut ties with Abu Dhabi on September 10 [3].

Algeria and Morocco, the two heavyweights of the Maghreb, have been in a cold war for decades, mainly because of Western Sahara, a territory that Morocco largely controls and that Algeria wants to see become independent [2].

This rivalry is costly: the two countries hardly trade with each other, and in 2021 Algeria stopped sending its gas to Spain through Morocco, by letting the contract for the Maghreb-Europe gas pipeline expire [5].
A "sabotage" case with no public details adds tension just as Algeria is also falling out with the Emirates. The risk: expulsions, retaliation, and even fewer chances of regional cooperation.

France has strong ties with both countries, and millions of people in France have family on both sides. When Algiers and Rabat quarrel, Paris is often caught in the crossfire, including on Algerian gas and visa issues.

news.2026-10-12-malaisie-brume-indonesie: Toxic haze: more than 600,000 pupils out of school in Malaysia because of Indonesian fires
Forest and peatland fires in Indonesia are sending thick smoke over Malaysia and Singapore. The neighbors are putting pressure on Jakarta.

The Malaysian state of Johor, next to Singapore, has extended the closure of all its schools from October 12 to 16, because the air pollution index remains stuck between 170 and 180, a level considered unhealthy [2]. At the first closure, this affected 1,198 schools and 617,258 pupils [3].

Indonesia faces growing pressure to punish polluters and accept more foreign help against the forest and peatland fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra; in Singapore, public aid against the haze takes effect on October 13 after a rise in emergency room visits [1].

Jakarta says it has mobilized 60,000 people against the fires, while Malaysia has offered one aircraft, three helicopters and 52 personnel and is still waiting for Indonesia's reply [4]. The number of fire hotspots has risen again, to 909, according to a count published on October 12 [6].

Smoke knows no borders: fires set in Indonesia close schools in Malaysia and fill emergency rooms in Singapore. According to Bloomberg, the episode is shaping up to be the worst in more than ten years, and the hotspots detected by satellite in September were at their highest since 2015 [5].

These fires are often linked to slash-and-burn farming, a technique that involves burning vegetation to clear land for agriculture, for example for plantations [1]. Peatlands, soils saturated with plant matter, burn for a long time and release enormous amounts of smoke and CO2.
It is a test for ASEAN, the club of Southeast Asian countries: Malaysia is calling for an emergency meeting of environment ministers, but Indonesia wants to keep control of its own crisis.

You are not breathing this smoke, but you may be consuming products linked to these lands: palm oil, paper, wood. This crisis is a reminder that deforestation on the other side of the world has very concrete effects on the health of millions of people and on everyone's climate.

news.2026-10-12-mexique-ouragan-simon-po: Hurricane Simon: Mexico closes nine ports, including its main gateway to Asia
Faced with a powerful hurricane on the Pacific coast, the Mexican Navy has closed Manzanillo, the country's top container port. Trade with Asia has come to a halt.

On Sunday, October 11, the Mexican Navy closed nine Pacific ports, including Manzanillo and Lázaro Cárdenas, as Hurricane Simon passed; 579 people were moved to shelters in the states of Jalisco, Colima and Nayarit [1].

The main container terminals in Manzanillo, including Contecon, SSA Marine and Hutchison Ports, had already suspended operations and postponed loading appointments to Monday, October 12 [3]. The airports of Puerto Vallarta and Manzanillo were also closed [5].
The eye of the hurricane stayed offshore and Simon weakened, but its rain and swell were enough to close the largest ports on Mexico's Pacific coast; no deaths were reported as of Monday morning [2].

Manzanillo is Mexico's top container port and its main entry point for goods coming from Asia [2]. In 2025, it handled nearly 3.9 million "twenty-foot equivalent" containers (TEU, the unit used to measure the metal boxes of world trade) [4].

When such a port stops, even for two or three days, ships wait offshore, parts do not reach factories and delays spread. Mexico has become a key workshop for American industry, notably the automotive sector.
With warmer oceans, intense hurricanes are becoming more frequent. Ports, often built on exposed coastlines, are on the front line.

The direct impact on you is small: Manzanillo mainly serves trade between Asia and North America. But this story shows how much our goods depend on a few big ports, and that a single storm can jam a supply chain on the other side of the world.
Pacific ports closed by the Mexican Navy
news.2026-10-12-bresil-paris-sportifs-in: Brazil: Lula bans sports betting, Flamengo and Fluminense play with a protest slogan
In Brazil, online sports betting has been banned since October 6. At the Rio derby, both clubs replaced their sponsor with "Banning is not protecting".

On Sunday, October 11, at the Maracanã stadium, Flamengo and Fluminense replaced the logo of their former betting sponsor (Betano and Superbet) on their shirts with the slogan "Proibir não é proteger" ("Banning is not protecting"), in protest against provisional measure 1,394/2026, which bans fixed-odds sports betting [1].

Signed by Lula on September 25, the text blocked new deposits and led to the shutdown of betting sites and apps on October 6; Congress must approve it within 120 days for it to remain in force [3]. The football federations of São Paulo and Rio called it a "fatal blow to Brazilian football", and Lula replied that the clubs "will have to manage on their own" [4].
The derby took place two weeks before the runoff of the presidential election on October 25, which turns this match into a political moment [2].

The government justifies the ban by gambling addiction and household over-indebtedness: according to the Finance Ministry, Brazilian households spend about 60 billion reais a year on online betting, while the sector brings in about 10 billion reais in taxes [3].
Operators respond that the ban will push more than 30 million bettors toward illegal sites, with no protection or taxes [3]. Football, for its part, suddenly loses its biggest sponsors.
This is a real choice for society, in the middle of a campaign: protect households or defend an industry that funds sport. The final decision will rest with Congress.

In France, online sports betting is legal and regulated by the National Gaming Authority (ANJ), and its ads are everywhere during matches. Brazil shows that a country can decide to stop everything at once: a debate that could one day reach us.

news.2026-10-12-danemark-robots-supermar: Denmark: humanoid robots learn to stock supermarket shelves at night
A supermarket near Copenhagen is testing human-shaped robots to restock shelves. The goal: for them to work alone at night by early 2027.
The Danish group Salling is testing humanoid robots in a Føtex supermarket near Copenhagen; they are developed by the Danish start-up Hive Robots on a base made by China's Unitree [1].

Training began in June 2026: human operators guide each movement so that the artificial intelligence learns to grasp and put away products, with the goal of autonomous restocking, mostly at night, by early 2027 [1].

According to Føtex, its employees spend 40 to 50% of their time stocking shelves; but the robots remain slower than humans, and Danish law is expected to change before they can work on their own among customers [2].
After factories, humanoid robots are starting to enter everyday service jobs. Stocking shelves is a repetitive and tiring task, which supermarkets struggle to staff at night.

Later, these robots could also check expiration dates and spot empty shelves or misplaced products [2]. The Salling group has more than 2,000 stores in six European countries, so a success could spread quickly [1].
The experiment also shows a dependence: the robot's "body" is Chinese, and only the software intelligence is European. It is an issue of industrial sovereignty.

Shelf-stocking jobs are often student jobs or first jobs. If these robots work, those positions could change, with fewer physical tasks and more machine supervision. Nothing is ready before 2027, but it is a trend to watch.
